Proposed Resolution for Joint Action to Redesign the Office of the Ombuds The Service and Community Life Committee (SCLC) December 12, 2024 Resolution The purpose of this resolution is to request immediate joint action by the Faculty Senate and the Office of the President as co-equal governing partners through the creation of a special joint committee.
The special joint committee will create a new Office of the Ombud.
Context In 2024, the Ombuds Dr.
Gerry Tyler and Dr.
Al Killilea were replaced by an Interim Ombud, Dr.
Charles Collyer.
An Interim Ombud role was created so that the Faculty Senate Service and Community Life Committee (SCLC), The Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC), and the office of Provost could take a year to redesign and re-establish a new Office of the Ombuds.
This resolution grows out of discussions that have taken place between SCLC, FSEC, and the Office of the Provost.

Expectations Membership of the special joint committee shall consist of advocates for those members of the campus community who may need or want to engage with the Office of the Ombuds: representatives from the faculty and delegates representing staff and student interests. ● Special joint committee co-chairs.
The committee shall be co-chaired by a designee from the SCLC and a designee from the Office of the President.
The co-chairs shall recruit committee members and manage and oversee the work of the committee until a new Office of the Ombuds is established. ● Committee charge.
The committee shall study best practices and decide the most appropriate actions for the design and creation of an effective Office of the Ombuds, including: ● Role, duties, powers and privileges.
The committee shall revise and update the policy that delineates the expectations of the Office of the Ombud and that codifies the duties, powers, and privileges of the Ombuds.

The position requires that the Ombuds are: ● Trained in how to listen and help identify issues and courses of action, mediate conflict or disputes, and guide and direct those in need ● Skilled and certified conflict mediators ● Connected to the university community, whether currently or formerly employed by the institution

● Provided equitable compensation for their work ● Provided with appropriate space ● Provided a community infrastructure, including but not limited to a cohort of others who work in the support system of the institution (CED, EEOC, Title 9, etc.) ● Job description, nomination, application and selection process. ● Job description.
The committee will develop a new job description that must convey the following critical ideas (per section 5.88.10 of the University Manual): the Ombud role shall be to: investigate complaints from students, faculty, and administrative personnel, with the very explicit charge to handle situations that fall outside of the auspices of the usual channels (such as the Office of Community, Equity, and Diversity, the unions, office of DEI in the respective colleges, EEOC, Title IX, and Human Resources).
The Ombuds are designated to handle primarily issues that stem from interpersonal conflicts. ● Application, hiring committee, and selection process.

The committee must also design a written application (whether it be an essay on qualifications and interest, or short answers to prompts) and an application and selection process that shall include a designated hiring committee.
The hiring committee shall include representatives of the university’s co-equal governing partnership: the Faculty Senate and the Office of the President.
The hiring committee shall review applications, interview candidates, and collectively make the final decision on the selection of at least two Ombuds.
It is important that there are at least two Ombuds, especially if they are full-time tenure track faculty, or faculty and staff, from two different colleges.
This allows for recusal from cases if necessary.
The SCLC recommends a two-person Office with one faculty representative and one staff representative. ● Nominations.

The Manual (5.88.11) indicates that The Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs and the Faculty Senate Executive Committee shall jointly nominate one or more full-time, tenured faculty or emeritus faculty for the post of Ombuds and shall submit the names of nominees to the Faculty Senate for confirmation, no later than May 1st of the year in which the Ombuds’ term is to begin.
Revisions must make certain that it is clear that nominations are not restricted to those put forth by any member of the administration and the Faculty Senate, but will follow the nomination and selection process designed and approved by

the special joint committee, which shall include the possibility of self-nominations. ● Visibility, privacy, and confidentiality. ● Physical space.
The committee must negotiate a new neutral space for the Office of the Ombuds that will achieve two critical goals: making the Office more visible to community members and also guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to enter that space to benefit from this valuable resource. ● Communication avenues.
The committee will be charged with designing communication avenues and reporting protocols that will guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to use this valuable resource. ● Digital space.
The committee will be responsible for the redesign of the Office of the Ombuds website to improve its online visibility so that the Office functions as the first stop in the reporting line.
The website must include clear messaging that is aligned with the University Manual, a more effective and reliable submission mechanism, clear expectations regarding potential courses of action and outcomes, and any other additional information that would enhance the user experience.

It would also be helpful to link the Office of the Ombuds to the other offices that handle certain student and personnel concerns, such Title IX and the CED office’s website, to increase visibility and clarity in messaging about its services.
This includes providing clear information about what the Office of the Ombuds does (and does not do).
This information is especially pertinent for new hires and newly admitted students, as well as providing ongoing messaging directed at URI employees and students. ● Reporting and Accountability.
Record keeping and reporting are critical features of a well-functioning ombud office. ● Case Reporting and Mechanisms of Accountability.
This committee must establish a policy about reporting cases, mechanisms of accountability, report storage, etc.
The reporting must not be compromised by the bureaucratic structure and must guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to use this valuable resource. ● Reporting and Accountability Cohort.
The committee must create an ecosystem/cohort of other staff who are working within reporting and resolution, such as the EEOC officer, Assistant Deans

focusing on DEI, the Office of Community Equity, and Diversity, Title 9 Officer, Dean of Students, representative from HR, among others. This cohort shall meet at least twice every semester. ● Consultancy. If supported financially, the committee will work with an outside consultancy to assist in the design and creation of the new office to achieve these goals.

FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES BS – Computer Science, effective Fall 2026 Appendix A The proposed curriculum revision modernizes the B.S. in Computer Science to reflect contemporary computing practice while maintaining academic rigor.
The revision introduces a formal specialization structure with focused pathways in Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity; and a flexible option, while streamlining major requirements to improve time-to-degree without reducing total credits or academic standards.
The specialization structure also allows for the addition of future specializations to meet the demand of this rapidly changing field.

We are proposing the following changes to major requirements: - Remove CSC 106, reducing time-to-degree by one semester. - Add CSC 310 as a core requirement, ensuring all graduates gain essential expertise in data -driven decision-making and AI/machine learning, skills that are now fundamental across all computing domains. - Remove MTH 142, acknowledging that MTH 141 provides sufficient mathematical foundation for required CS courses. - Add STA 409 to ensure consistent mathematical preparation for machine learning, data analysis, and advanced study in artificial intelligence. - Reduce the science requirement from two courses to one, allowing expanded free electives while maintaining interdisciplinary science exposure. - Refine the writing requirement course list to align with general education requirements. - Implement formal specializations in Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, and General Computer Science, replacing loosely defined electives with coherent learning pathways aligned with high -demand employment sectors.

This curriculum revision strengthens the Computer Science major through internal reallocation of Department resources rather than expansion.
The proposed changes maintain the same total credit requirements (120 credits, 56 in major) while improving student outcomes through streamlined prerequisites and providing clearer career pathways via formal specializations in the two highest-growth computing sectors: Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity.
For students, the revision delivers a contemporary curriculum that reflects current industry practice without compromising academic rigor.
For the Department, the changes ensure alignment with national curriculum standards, facilitate enrollment management through reduced bottlenecks, and enhance recruitment by offering competitive specializations in the technology industry's most in-demand areas.
The clear program structure with AI and Cybersecurity pathways strengthens program identity for accreditation, assessment, and marketing to prospective students.

For the University, the revision supports improved graduation rates, responds directly to workforce demand for specialized computing skills, and strengthens the institution's position in a highly competitive academic market.

Specialization – Artificial Intelligence (CSC BS) Appendix B The specialization in Artificial Intelligence equips students with a progressive pathway from core machine learning concepts through advanced topics in deep learning, large language models, statistical learning, and scalable data algorithms.

Anchored by CSC 461 (Machine Learning) as a required gateway course, the specialization ensures that every student develops foundational competency in machine learning before advancing to two upper-division electives drawn from a curated menu spanning neural networks and deep learning (CSC 561), big data algorithms (CSC 546), multivariate statistical learning (STA 441), and special topics in AI (CSC 581).
We are in the process of reactivating artificial intelligence (CSC 481), which was removed from the catalog because it had not been taught recently.
We plan to add it to the rotation of courses once it is reactivated.
Additionally, we have 2 new courses in the Kuali pipeline, large language models (CSC 455) and machine learning security and privacy (CSC 465).
These courses have been taught in the last couple of years as special topics (CSC 492/592) for undergraduate and graduate students.
Until these courses are approved, students can use them to fulfill requirements with departmental permission.

Built on the program's core computer science requirements, this three -course specialization delivers the theoretical depth and applied judgment graduates need to design, evaluate, and responsibly deploy intelligent systems across diverse computing domains.
The specialization directly implements recent trends in CS education, which identify machine learning and artificial intelligence as central knowledge areas for contemporary CS graduates and implement coherent depth pathways beyond introductory ML/AI expos ure.
Critically, this specialization reflects a fundamental shift in the discipline itself: artificial intelligence is no longer a peripheral subfield, it is now core to how software systems are designed, deployed, and evaluated across virtually every application domain.
The strongest AI practitioners are not narrow specialists but professionals with deep computer science foundations in algorithms, systems, and software design, precisely what this program's core curriculum provides.

The timeliness of this specialization cannot be overstated.
AI and machine learning consistently rank among the highest-demand and highest-compensating skills in the computing workforce, and regional employers, from healthcare and defense to financial services and technology, are actively seeking graduates with exactly this preparation.
Peer institutions across New England have already established formal AI tracks or majors, and the absence of a comparable pathway at URI places the program at a direct competitive disadvantage in student recruitment.
Importantly, the Department has made investments in faculty with expertise in machine learning, data science, and AI over recent years.
This specialization now formally leverages these investments into a coherent, marketable academic pathway for undergraduate students.
Specialization – Cyber Security (CSC BS) Appendix C The Cybersecurity specialization provides students with a structured pathway from foundational security concepts to advanced defensive practice.

CSF 430 establishes core knowledge of security threats, defensive planning, and implementation of protective technologies, while CSF 432 builds hands-on competency in securing the networks and systems of real-world organizations.
Students then complete either CSF 434 or CSF 534, both of which advance into specialized topics including intrusion detection, penetration testing, incident response, malware analysis, and risk management, with CSF 534 incorporating a research dimension suited to students pursuing graduate study.
The Department of Computer Science and Statistics has developed substantial curricular expertise in cybersecurity over many years, reflected in a well-established sequence of CSF courses that, until now, have not been formally integrated into the B.S. in Computer Science.
This specialization rectifies that gap by leveraging existing departmental resources, faculty expertise, course infrastructure, and proven instructional design to offer students a coherent, named credential without requiring new courses or additional hiring.

This is particularly timely given that cybersecurity professionals are among the most critically needed in today's workforce and organizations across every sector face a widening shortage of qualified security professionals.
By formally establishing this specialization, the Department positions its graduates to meet this demand while enhancing the University's competitiveness in recruiting students who seek purposeful, career -aligned computing education.
Specialization – General Computer Science (CSC BS) Appendix D The General Computer Science specialization provides students with a structured yet flexible pathway to tailor advanced coursework to their individual interests and career goals.
Building on the program's core curriculum, students complete three additional CSC courses: one at the 300 level or above and two at the 400 level or above.
Our department currently offers many eligible courses in areas that include, but are not limited to, algorithms, artificial intelligence, computer graphics, database systems, computer systems, programming languages, and networking.

This specialization enables students to develop both depth and breadth beyond the core curriculum while aligning their studies with departmental strengths, emerging technologies, and evolving workforce demands.
Because no single specialization can encompass the full scope of modern computing, the General Computer Science pathway preserves student access to the discipline’s broad intellectual landscape.
It ensures that students whose goals lie outside established options such as Artificial Intelligence or Cybersecurity can still pursue a formally recognized course of study.
In doing so, the specialization supports preparation for diverse computing careers, interdisciplinary work, and graduate study across the field.
